title: 7 Best CRMs for Google Workspace in 2026
summary: Compare seven CRMs for Google Workspace, with Octolane as our top AI CRM pick. See Gmail and Calendar workflows, trade-offs, and a practical trial checklist.
body_markdown:
## Which CRM should you use with Google Workspace?


Octolane is our first recommendation for a team that runs sales through Gmail and Google Calendar and wants AI to help keep the CRM current. If your priority is working entirely inside Gmail, start by evaluating Streak. If marketing forms and campaigns drive your pipeline, include HubSpot in your shortlist.


The right choice depends on what you expect the CRM to do after it connects to Google. Logging an email, creating a contact, preparing a meeting, and drafting the next response are separate jobs. A Google integration badge does not tell you which of them the product handles.


This guide compares seven options by their documented capabilities and the workflows they suit. We publish Octolane, and the ordering reflects our preference for reducing manual sales administration. This is an editorial shortlist, not an independent benchmark or a claim that we ran every product through the same test. Product documentation was reviewed in September 2026.


## The shortlist at a glance


- **1. Octolane:** our pick for AI-assisted sales work across Gmail, meetings, and the CRM.
- **2. Streak:** for teams that want their pipeline inside Gmail.
- **3. Copper:** for relationship work alongside Gmail and Google Calendar.
- **4. HubSpot:** for teams combining inbound lead capture with a CRM.
- **5. Pipedrive:** for deal and activity management with email and calendar sync.
- **6. folk:** for a shared view of contacts and relationship history.
- **7. Salesflare:** for B2B teams prioritizing automatic activity capture and follow-up reminders.


The sections below explain what to check before committing to each one. Several of these products include AI features. The useful distinction is the work they can perform with your data, on the plan you intend to buy.


## What “works with Google Workspace” should mean


Before comparing products, write down the Google services your team uses and what you need to happen in each one.


**Gmail:** Should the CRM import historical messages, log new conversations, send replies, or appear inside the inbox? Ask how aliases, shared addresses, and private conversations are handled. Those are different requirements from connecting one personal mailbox.


**Google Calendar:** Decide whether you need one-way visibility or two-way updates. Check rescheduled meetings, cancellations, recurring events, and private appointments. An integration that shows an upcoming meeting may not write changes back to Google.


**Google Contacts:** Find out whether the CRM imports contacts, sends changes back, or simply creates its own records from email participants. Check duplicate behavior before importing a large address book.


**Drive and Sheets:** If documents and spreadsheets are part of your sales process, ask for the exact workflow. Linking a Drive file, searching its contents, and importing a Sheet are separate capabilities. Do not assume they come with Gmail sync.


**Google Meet:** Verify whether the product records or transcribes meetings, how participation works, and where the resulting notes go. Calendar access alone does not answer those questions.


## 1. Octolane: our pick for AI-led sales on Google Workspace


Octolane is built for teams that want help doing the ongoing work of sales: keeping records current, preparing for meetings, and following up with the right context. Its published plans include Gmail and Google Calendar sync, meeting preparation, follow-up drafting, and AI field updates. The level of autonomous action varies by plan. Check[Octolane's plans](https://www.octolane.com/pricing) for the workflow you need.


For a founder, the useful test is concrete. After several calls and a busy inbox, can you find the commitments that still need attention? Can the CRM help prepare the next message and reflect what changed in the deal?


Our customer stories show how teams describe using it.[Quivly's founder](https://www.octolane.com/customers/octolane-customer-quivly) uses meeting preparation, custom Skills for Granola transcript analysis, and AI fields in her sales workflow.[Respan's team](https://www.octolane.com/customers/respan-revenue-superintelligence) describes using Octolane to surface follow-ups and draft messages in their own voice. These are reported customer experiences, not promises about every deployment.


**Best fit:** a founder or sales team that already has conversations in Gmail and wants to spend less time maintaining the system around them.


**Check in your trial:** connect an appropriate sample of your sales data and ask for outstanding follow-ups. Review the source context, the suggested next steps, and a draft response. Confirm what needs your approval and which actions the selected plan can take automatically. Test any required Drive, Contacts, shared-inbox, or external-tool workflow separately.


## 2. Streak: for running a pipeline inside Gmail


Streak puts CRM pipelines in Gmail. Its product documentation describes email logging, pipeline tracking, tasks, and mail merge, along with AI features for working with CRM data. It is a sensible option to evaluate when staying inside the inbox matters more than introducing a separate sales workspace. See[Streak's product overview](https://www.streak.com/) .


**Best fit:** a small team that wants to review messages and move relationships through a pipeline in the same interface.


**Check in your trial:** work through a real email thread, update a deal, and ask a teammate to pick it up. Test the mobile experience and team visibility as well as the desktop extension. Make sure your reporting needs fit the workflow before committing to an inbox-centered setup.


## 3. Copper: for relationship work alongside Google apps


Copper's Chrome extension brings relationship context and CRM actions into Gmail and Google Calendar, and also supports LinkedIn workflows. Its documentation covers contact information, templates, and tasks in the extension. That makes it worth evaluating when you want the CRM available beside your existing Google workflow. See[Copper's extension guide](https://support.copper.com/en/articles/15851590-manage-relationship-with-the-chrome-extension) .


**Best fit:** a relationship-focused team that wants to look up context and manage follow-through while working in Google apps.


**Check in your trial:** open a contact from Gmail, review an upcoming meeting, and create a task. Ask which actions work in the extension and which require the full CRM. Have a second teammate check what context is shared and what stays private.


## 4. HubSpot: for inbound marketing and sales in one system


HubSpot is worth considering when lead capture and sales need a shared database. Its forms can create or update CRM records. It also supports connected Gmail accounts and a Google Calendar integration, with setup requirements and behavior documented separately. See the official guides for[forms](https://knowledge.hubspot.com/forms/create-and-edit-forms) ,[connected email](https://knowledge.hubspot.com/connected-email/connect-your-inbox-to-hubspot) , and[calendar sync](https://knowledge.hubspot.com/integrations/use-hubspots-integration-with-google-calendar-or-outlook-calendar) .


**Best fit:** a team that wants to follow a lead from a marketing form into a sales conversation.


**Check in your trial:** submit a form, verify the contact record, send a reply, and book a meeting. Price the complete workflow you need across products, seats, automation, and contact tiers. Confirm which capabilities are included before treating an entry-level plan as the total cost.


## 5. Pipedrive: for deal and activity management


Pipedrive supports Gmail email sync, calendar sync, Google Contacts sync, and a Google Drive integration. Its current email documentation also describes AI summaries and drafting tools. Google Calendar sync can be configured one-way or two-way. See[Pipedrive's Google integration overview](https://support.pipedrive.com/en/article/syncing-with-your-email-calendar-or-contacts-provider) ,[email sync documentation](https://support.pipedrive.com/en/article/email-sync) , and[calendar behavior](https://support.pipedrive.com/en/article/calendar-sync) .


**Best fit:** a team that wants deals, activities, and email conversations organized around a sales pipeline.


**Check in your trial:** connect a mailbox, attach a thread to the correct deal, and reschedule an activity from Google Calendar. Review the documented handling of recurring and private events. Confirm the plan that includes email sync and any automation you require.


## 6. folk: for shared contacts and relationship history


folk imports Google contacts and associates email and calendar interactions with contact profiles. Its documentation describes Google Contacts import as one-way: changes in folk do not sync back into Google Contacts. It also documents exclusions for certain messages and events. See[folk's Google import guide](https://help.folk.app/en/articles/4970606-import-contacts-from-google) .


**Best fit:** a team that wants to organize a relationship network and see relevant interaction history together.


**Check in your trial:** import a representative group of contacts, inspect several message histories, and confirm the sharing settings. Include a recurring event and an archived message in the test because the documented import exclusions may matter to your workflow. Check how much historical data your plan makes available.


## 7. Salesflare: for B2B activity capture and reminders


Salesflare describes its CRM as collecting relationship information with less manual entry. Its product overview includes Gmail integration, automated reminders, visual pipelines, and email sequences. It is worth evaluating if keeping activity history current is the main reason your team is replacing a spreadsheet or an older CRM. See[Salesflare's product overview](https://salesflare.com/) .


**Best fit:** a small B2B team that wants help tracking conversations and remembering when to follow up.


**Check in your trial:** inspect which contacts and activities appear automatically, then trace a reminder back to the underlying conversation. Confirm Google Calendar behavior and distinguish built-in capabilities from workflows that need an integration service. Test a handoff between two teammates, not just one connected inbox.


## How to compare them without spending weeks in demos


Use the same small set of records in each trial. A useful test pack includes a new prospect, an existing customer, two people at the same company, a stale deal, and a private conversation that should remain private.


### Test the complete conversation


Send a message, receive a reply, book a meeting, and reschedule it. Check which steps appear in the CRM and which require intervention. Inspect both the contact and company records so you can see whether the relationship is being represented correctly.


Do not stop when the inbox connection says “connected.” The important result is whether the right information reaches the right record.


### Test a missed commitment


Include a message where you promised to send something by a particular day. See how the CRM helps you recover that obligation. Does it show the conversation? Create a reminder? Suggest a next step? Draft a response?


Write down the steps you still have to perform. This makes different approaches to automation easier to compare without reducing the decision to an “AI: yes or no” checkbox.


### Test team access and departure


Have a colleague open the same account and check what they can see. Review how private messages, shared records, and account ownership are handled. Ask what happens when a teammate disconnects their Google account or leaves the company.


Your Workspace administrator should be involved in approving the connection and reviewing its access. Use the vendor's current setup instructions, and verify the configuration with your own account policies.


### Test recovery and export


Disconnect and reconnect a test mailbox. Check for missing or duplicate records. Export a small set of contacts, companies, and deals, then inspect which custom fields and relationships survive.


A trial is also the time to learn what happens when a sync fails. Ask where errors appear, who receives an alert, and how to retry without duplicating work.


## What should you budget for?


Compare the monthly cost of the workflow your team will actually run. That can include seats, connected accounts, AI usage, enrichment, automation, marketing contacts, add-ons, and the time someone spends administering the system.


For example, a hypothetical five-person team paying $30 per person would start at $150 per month before extras. If a required feature sits on another tier, that starting calculation no longer describes your purchase. This is an illustration, not a quoted price for any product in this guide.


Ask each vendor to confirm the same list of requirements. Record the billing period, limits, and any implementation cost. That gives you a comparable estimate without relying on a headline price that covers a different use case.


## A practical migration plan


Keep an export of the old CRM before moving data. Agree on the fields and stages you want to keep, and use a small sample to check contacts, company relationships, deal values, owners, and conversation history.


Choose which system your team will update during the transition. Running two live pipelines without clear ownership can create conflicting records. After the import, compare counts and inspect a sample from each stage before inviting everyone to work in the new system.


Then repeat the email, meeting, and follow-up tests. Import success and day-to-day usefulness are separate checks.


## Choose around the work you want to stop doing


If maintaining records and remembering next steps are the main problems, start with[Octolane](https://www.octolane.com/pricing) and test that workflow with your own conversations. If your strongest requirement is a pipeline inside Gmail, include Streak. If forms and marketing handoffs dominate the process, include HubSpot.


Your final choice should make a normal sales day easier to run. After a week, check whether the team can find context, trust the records, and follow through with less manual work. Those answers will tell you more than the length of an integration list.
